fetched_contents.text: Screening for Cervical Cancer | Cervical Cancer * The HPV test and the Pap test can help prevent cervical cancer or find it early. * You should start getting Pap tests at age 21. If you are 30 years old or older, talk to your doctor about testing options. Screening tests The HPV test and the Pap test can help prevent cervical cancer or find it early. * The HPV test looks for the virus (human papillomavirus) that can cause cell changes on the cervix. * The Pap test (or Pap smear) looks for precancers, cell changes on the cervix that might become cervical cancer if they are not treated appropriately. Both tests can be done in a doctor's office or clinic. During the Pap test, the doctor will use a plastic or metal instrument, called a speculum, to look inside your vagina. This helps the doctor examine the vagina and the cervix, and collect a few cells and mucus from the cervix and the area around it. The cells are sent to a laboratory. * If you are getting a Pap test, the cells will be checked to see if they look normal. * If you are getting an HPV test, the cells will be tested for HPV. What is cervical precancer? When there are cervical cells that look abnormal but are not yet cancerous, it is called cervical precancer. These abnormal cells may be the first sign of cancer that develops years later. Cervical precancer usually doesn't cause pain or other symptoms. It is found with a Pap test. Cindy's Story: Preventing Cervical Cancer This video tells the story of Cindy, who took action after precancerous cells were found during her routine cervical cancer screening. A 30-second version is also available: watch or download [1MB]. When to get screened If you are 21 to 29 years old You should start getting Pap tests at age 21. If your Pap test result is normal, your doctor may tell you that you can wait three years until your next Pap test. If you are 30 to 65 years old Talk to your doctor about which testing option is right for you: * An HPV test only. This is called primary HPV testing. If your result is normal, your doctor may tell you that you can wait five years until your next screening test. * An HPV test along with a Pap test. This is called co-testing. If both of your results are normal, your doctor may tell you that you can wait five years until your next screening test. * A Pap test only. If your result is normal, your doctor may tell you that you can wait three years until your next Pap test. If you are older than 65 Your doctor may tell you that you don't need to be screened anymore if: * You have had at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years, and the test results were normal or negative, and * You have not had a cervical precancer in the past, or * You have had your cervix removed as part of a total hysterectomy for non-cancerous conditions, like fibroids. Are you worried about the cost?‎‎ CDC offers free or low-cost cervical cancer screening tests through the National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program. How to prepare for your test No special preparation is needed before you have an HPV test. If you are getting a Pap test, you can take steps to make sure the test results are accurate. Avoid intercourse, douching, and using vaginal medicines or spermicidal foam for 2 days before the test. If you had sex before the test, go to the appointment as planned and let the doctor know. If you have your period, don't worry. Both tests can still be done at this time. Test results It can take as long as three weeks to receive your test results. If your test shows that something might not be normal, your doctor will contact you and figure out how best to follow up. There are many reasons why test results might not be normal. It usually does not mean you have cancer. If your test results show cells that are not normal and may become cancer, your doctor will let you know if you need to be treated. In most cases, treatment prevents cervical cancer from developing. It is important to follow up with your doctor right away to learn more about your test results and receive any treatment that may be needed. If your test results are normal, your chance of getting cervical cancer in the next few years is very low. Your doctor may tell you that you can wait several years for your next cervical cancer screening test. But you should still go to the doctor regularly for a checkup. Pap test result A Pap test result can be normal, unclear, abnormal, or unsatisfactory. * A normal (or "negative") result means that no cell changes were found on your cervix. This is good news. But you still need to get Pap tests in the future. New cell changes can still form on your cervix. Your doctor may tell you that you can wait three years for your next screening test if you received a Pap test only. If you also received an HPV test, and the result is negative, your doctor may tell you that you can wait five years for your next screening test. * It is common for test results to come back unclear. Your doctor may use other words to describe this result, like equivocal, inconclusive, or ASC-US. These all mean the same thing—that your cervical cells look like they could be abnormal. It is not clear if it's related to HPV. It could be related to life changes like pregnancy, menopause, or an infection. The HPV test can help find out if your cell changes are related to HPV. Ask your doctor what to do next. * An abnormal result means that cell changes were found on your cervix. This usually does not mean that you have cervical cancer. Abnormal changes on your cervix are likely caused by HPV. The changes may be minor (low-grade) or serious (high-grade). Most of the time, minor changes go back to normal on their own. But more serious changes can turn into cancer if they are not removed. The more serious changes are often called "precancer" because they are not yet cancer, but they can turn into cancer over time. Mini-report on when to stop cervical cancer screening and what changes the schedule

The evidence points to two main age thresholds for stopping screening: 65 years and adequate prior screening history. For average-risk women older than 65 years, the USPSTF says screening is not recommended if they have had adequate prior screening and are not otherwise at high risk for cervical cancer [N2-F2]. NCBI also states that clinicians should stop screening average-risk women older than 65 years if they have had 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cytology plus HPV test results within 10 years, with the most recent test performed within 5 years [N3-F3]. The CDC similarly states that women older than 65 may not need screening if they have had at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years with normal or negative results and no cervical precancer [N1-F1].

HPV status is not the only determinant of stopping screening, but it can affect the evidence base for stopping. USPSTF says adequate prior screening is the main criterion, not just HPV status alone [N2-F2]. NCBI says a negative HPV test can provide greater reassurance of low CIN3+ risk than a negative cytology result, but stopping screening depends on adequate prior screening and not just HPV result [N3-F3]. The CDC also says adequate prior screening is the main condition for stopping screening after age 65 [N1-F1]. So HPV status may support a decision to stop screening if it is part of an adequate prior screening history, but it is not a standalone stopping rule.

What changes the recommended schedule? The evidence identifies three main factors: age, prior test results, and whether a woman has had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix. USPSTF says screening should not be done in women who have had a hysterectomy with removal of the cervix and no history of a high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer [N2-F2]. NCBI says clinicians should not screen average-risk women younger than 21 years, and women aged 25–65 can be screened every 5 years with HPV alone or co-testing, while women aged 21–29 are screened every 3 years with cytology alone [N3-F3]. The CDC adds that women aged 21 to 29 should start Pap tests at age 21 and be screened every 3 years, while women aged 30 to 65 can choose HPV-only every 5 years or co-testing every 5 years, and women older than 65 may stop screening if they have adequate prior negative tests [N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that abnormal results can change the schedule: if a Pap or HPV result is abnormal, follow-up testing is needed sooner than the regular interval [N4-F2].

Overall, the schedule changes when a woman reaches age 65, has adequate prior negative tests, has had a hysterectomy with cervix removal, or has abnormal screening results [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F2].

Mini-report on recommended screening intervals

The evidence is consistent on age groups and how often screening is recommended. USPSTF says women aged 21 to 29 should be screened every 3 years with cytology alone, and women aged 30 to 65 should be screened every 5 years with HPV testing alone or co-testing [N2-F2]. CDC says women aged 21 to 29 should start Pap tests at age 21 and be screened every 3 years, while women aged 30 to 65 can choose HPV-only every 5 years or co-testing every 5 years [N1-F1]. NCI similarly states that women aged 30 to 65 should be screened with HPV testing every 5 years or co-testing every 5 years [N1-R4]. The evidence also notes that women aged 21 to 29 may be screened every 3 years with cytology alone, and women aged 25 to 65 can be screened every 5 years with HPV alone or co-testing [N3-F3].

How Pap test and HPV test intervals differ by age and co-testing status is clear. For women aged 21 to 29, the evidence favors cytology alone every 3 years, with no routine HPV testing [N1-F1][N3-F3]. For women aged 30 to 65, HPV testing alone every 5 years is one option, and co-testing every 5 years is preferred [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The CDC also notes that Pap-only screening can be repeated every 3 years, while HPV-only screening can be repeated every 5 years [N1-F1]. The evidence further states that co-testing is an option in maximal settings, but the added value on the basis of increased costs is limited [N3-F3].

When to repeat testing and when to skip a test is tied to normal results. The evidence says that after a normal Pap test alone, a woman may wait 3 years until the next Pap test [N1-F1]. After a normal HPV test alone, a woman may wait 5 years until the next screening test [N1-F1]. After both Pap and HPV tests are normal, a woman may wait 5 years for co-testing [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that adequate screening is defined as 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative HPV results within 10 years [N3-R1]. This means that if a woman has normal results repeatedly, she may skip a test for the next interval, but she should not skip the next interval if she has not met the repeat-test threshold.

In summary, screening intervals depend on age and test type: every 3 years for cytology alone in women aged 21–29, every 5 years for HPV alone or co-testing in women aged 30–65, and the schedule may be adjusted or skipped only after repeated normal results [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R1].

Mini-report on HPV-negative versus HPV-positive management differences

The evidence shows that HPV-negative results can change screening frequency and reduce the urgency of follow-up. USPSTF says adequate prior screening is the main criterion for stopping screening, not just HPV status alone [N2-F2]. NCBI states that a negative HPV test provides greater reassurance of low CIN3+ risk than a negative cytology result, but stopping screening depends on adequate prior screening and not just HPV result [N3-F3]. CDC similarly says women may wait longer after normal HPV tests because HPV-negative results can be used for longer intervals [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that if HPV is negative and a Pap test is normal, the next screening can be repeated every 5 years [N1-F1]. So HPV-negative results are associated with less frequent follow-up and can support a longer interval, but they do not override the need for adequate prior screening history.

HPV-positive results affect follow-up and testing more directly. USPSTF says clinicians should not screen women younger than 21 years, and HPV testing is recommended in all resource settings [N3-F3]. NCI states that if HPV is positive, the next test should be done sooner, and referral to colposcopy is recommended if HPV is positive at the 1-year follow-up visit [N4-R4]. ACOG notes that repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year is recommended for patients with minor screening abnormalities indicating HPV [N4-R1]. The evidence also suggests that HPV-positive women may need more immediate attention, including colposcopy, because positive HPV status is a marker of increased risk [N4-R4][N4-R1].

What screening changes when HPV is positive? The evidence indicates that HPV-positive results typically shorten the next-testing interval. NCI says if HPV is positive, the next test should be done sooner and may require colposcopy [N4-R4]. ACOG recommends repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year after minor abnormalities [N4-R1]. The evidence also suggests that HPV-positive women should be followed more closely, including referral to colposcopy, and that HPV-positive women may need more frequent or earlier evaluation [N4-R4][N4-R1]. In other words, HPV-positive results usually mean a more urgent follow-up plan rather than skipping a test.

Overall, HPV-negative results can support longer intervals and may reduce the urgency of follow-up, while HPV-positive results usually mean shorter follow-up intervals, earlier repeat testing, and a higher likelihood of referral to colposcopy [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R1][N4-R4].

Mini-report on practical patient guidance and next steps

To explain the schedule in simple terms, the evidence recommends starting with the basics: screening starts at age 21, and women aged 21–29 are tested every 3 years with Pap only. Women aged 30–65 can choose HPV-only every 5 years or co-testing every 5 years [N1-F1][N2-F2]. For older women, if they have had enough normal tests, screening may stop after age 65 [N1-F1]. The evidence also says that after normal results, a woman may wait 3 years for Pap-only or 5 years for HPV-only [N1-F1]. This can be explained as “wait longer if your test is normal,” with the exact wait time depending on the test used [N1-F1].

If a Pap/HPV result is abnormal, the evidence points to next steps that are not just waiting for the next scheduled test. NCI says abnormal results usually do not mean cancer, but they do mean follow-up is needed [N6-R3]. It also says that if HPV is positive, the next test should be sooner and that referral to colposcopy is recommended [N4-R4]. ACOG says repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year is recommended for patients with minor screening abnormalities indicating HPV [N4-R1]. CDC similarly says that if results are abnormal, the doctor will contact the patient and figure out the best follow-up, and that abnormal changes are usually caused by HPV [N1-F1]. So the practical next step after an abnormal result is to see a provider for evaluation, not just wait longer.

When to see a provider for further evaluation is tied to abnormal results and HPV positivity. The evidence says that if results are abnormal, the doctor will contact the patient and determine next steps [N1-F1]. It also says that referral to colposcopy is recommended if cytology results are abnormal or if HPV is positive at the 1-year follow-up visit [N4-R4]. ACOG similarly recommends repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year after minor abnormalities [N4-R1]. Therefore, the provider is the next step after abnormal results, especially if HPV is positive or if the result is unclear [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R4].

In simple language, the guidance is: start screening at age 21, have tests every 3 years if you are 21–29, every 5 years if you are 30–65, and may stop after age 65 if you have enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2]. If a result is abnormal, go back sooner and see your provider for evaluation, especially if HPV is positive [N4-R1][N4-R4][N6-R3].

# Final answer: How often should you get the Pap test and HPV test?

If you’re asking “no sé cada cuánto me debo hacer la prueba de Papanicolau y de HPV,” the short answer is: the schedule depends on your age and your test results, but the general guidelines are simple and clear.

## 1) Age groups and how often screening is recommended
The evidence is consistent across the guidelines.  
- **Women aged 21 to 29 years**: you should be screened every **3 years** with **Pap testing alone** [N2-F2][N1-F1].  
- **Women aged 30 to 65 years**: you can choose **HPV testing alone every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Women older than 65 years**: screening may stop if you have had **enough normal tests in the past**, usually **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

So the core schedule is:
- **21–29 years**: every 3 years with Pap only.
- **30–65 years**: every 5 years with HPV alone or co-testing.
- **Over 65 years**: screening may stop if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 2) How Pap test and HPV test intervals differ by age and co-testing status
The main difference is that **Pap-only screening is shorter than HPV-only screening** in some age groups.

- **Women aged 21–29 years**: the guidelines recommend **Pap only every 3 years**, and routine HPV testing is not recommended in this group [N1-F1][N3-F3].  
- **Women aged 30–65 years**: the choice is **HPV-only every 5 years** or **co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Co-testing** is preferred for women aged 30–65 because it combines Pap and HPV results and may offer better reassurance in some settings [N2-F2][N3-F3].  

In other words, the interval is usually **every 3 years** if you have Pap only in younger women, and **every 5 years** if you use HPV alone or co-testing in older women [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 3) When to repeat testing and when to skip a test
The evidence says that if your test result is **normal**, you may **wait the full interval** before the next test.  
- After a **normal Pap test alone**, you may wait **3 years** until the next Pap test [N1-F1].  
- After a **normal HPV test alone**, you may wait **5 years** until the next screening test [N1-F1].  
- After both tests are **normal**, you may wait **5 years** for co-testing [N1-F1].  

But this is only true if your results are normal. If your result is **abnormal**, you should **not wait for the next scheduled test**—you should see your provider sooner, and sometimes you may need more frequent follow-up [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-F1].

## 4) When to stop cervical cancer screening and what changes the schedule
The main age threshold for stopping screening is **65 years**, but it depends on your prior screening history.  
- USPSTF says screening should **not be done** in women older than 65 years who have had **adequate prior screening** and are not otherwise at high risk [N2-F2].  
- NCBI says clinicians should stop screening average-risk women older than 65 years if they have had **3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cytology plus HPV test results within 10 years**, with the most recent test performed within 5 years [N3-F3].  
- CDC similarly says women older than 65 may not need screening if they have had **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results and no cervical precancer [N1-F1].  

So the schedule changes when:
- You reach age 65.
- You have had enough normal tests in the past.
- You have had a **hysterectomy with removal of the cervix** and no high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer [N2-F2].
- Your results are abnormal or you have other risk factors [N2-F2][N4-F2].

## 5) Practical patient guidance: how to explain the schedule in simple terms
You can explain it like this:  
- Start screening at **age 21**.  
- If you are **21–29 years old**, get a **Pap test every 3 years**.  
- If you are **30–65 years old**, you can choose **HPV testing every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years**.  
- If you are **older than 65**, you may **not need screening anymore** if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

If your result is **normal**, you can wait the full interval before your next test. If it’s **abnormal**, you should **see your provider sooner** [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 6) What to do if a Pap/HPV result is abnormal
The evidence is clear: abnormal results do **not** mean cancer, but they do mean **follow-up is needed** [N6-R3][N1-F1].  
- If your **Pap or HPV result is abnormal**, your provider will explain the next steps and determine whether you need more testing sooner [N1-F1][N6-R3].  
- If HPV is **positive**, follow-up is usually more urgent: you may need to come back **sooner** and may be referred to **colposcopy** [N4-R4].  
- ACOG also says **repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year** is recommended for minor abnormalities indicating HPV [N4-R1].  

So the next step after an abnormal result is to:
1. See your provider.
2. Follow their instructions for repeat testing or further evaluation.
3. Understand that abnormal results usually mean follow-up, not a cancer diagnosis [N6-R3][N4-R4].

## 7) When to see a provider for further evaluation
You should see a provider after an **abnormal result** or if HPV is **positive** [N4-R4][N1-F1].  
- If your result is abnormal, the provider will contact you and decide what to do next [N1-F1].  
- If HPV is positive, the provider may recommend **colposcopy** or earlier repeat testing [N4-R4].  
- If you have other risk factors, a history of abnormal results, or a hysterectomy with cervix removal, your provider may also change your schedule [N2-F2][N3-F3].

## 8) HPV-negative versus HPV-positive management differences
The evidence shows that HPV status can change how you are followed.  
- **HPV-negative results** can support longer intervals and less urgent follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F3].  
- **HPV-positive results** usually mean shorter follow-up intervals, earlier repeat testing, and a higher chance of referral to **colposcopy** [N4-R4][N4-R1].  

So:
- If HPV is negative and your Pap is normal, you can wait longer before the next test.
- If HPV is positive, you may need to come back sooner and may need more testing or evaluation [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 9) Bottom line for the patient
If you want to know how often you should get the **Pap test and HPV test**, the answer is:

- **Start at age 21**.
- **21–29 years**: every **3 years** with Pap only.
- **30–65 years**: every **5 years** with HPV alone or co-testing.
- **Over 65 years**: screening may stop if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **If a result is normal**, you can wait the full interval before your next test.
- **If a result is abnormal or HPV is positive**, you should see your provider sooner [N1-F1][N4-R4].

In simple terms:  
**Normal results = wait the full time. Abnormal results = see your provider sooner.**

# Final answer: How often should you get the Pap test and HPV test?

If you’re asking “no sé cada cuánto me debo hacer la prueba de Papanicolau y de HPV,” the short answer is: the schedule depends on your age and your test results, but the general guidelines are simple and clear.

## 1) Age groups and how often screening is recommended
The evidence is consistent across the guidelines.  
- **Women aged 21 to 29 years**: you should be screened every **3 years** with **Pap testing alone** [N2-F2][N1-F1].  
- **Women aged 30 to 65 years**: you can choose **HPV testing alone every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Women older than 65 years**: screening may stop if you have had **enough normal tests in the past**, usually **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

So the core schedule is:
- **21–29 years**: every 3 years with Pap only.
- **30–65 years**: every 5 years with HPV alone or co-testing.
- **Over 65 years**: screening may stop if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 2) How Pap test and HPV test intervals differ by age and co-testing status
The main difference is that **Pap-only screening is shorter than HPV-only screening** in some age groups.

- **Women aged 21–29 years**: the guidelines recommend **Pap only every 3 years**, and routine HPV testing is not recommended in this group [N1-F1][N3-F3].  
- **Women aged 30–65 years**: the choice is **HPV-only every 5 years** or **co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Co-testing** is preferred for women aged 30–65 because it combines Pap and HPV results and may offer better reassurance in some settings [N2-F2][N3-F3].  

In other words, the interval is usually **every 3 years** if you have Pap only in younger women, and **every 5 years** if you use HPV alone or co-testing in older women [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 3) When to repeat testing and when to skip a test
The evidence says that if your test result is **normal**, you may **wait the full interval** before the next test.  
- After a **normal Pap test alone**, you may wait **3 years** until the next Pap test [N1-F1].  
- After a **normal HPV test alone**, you may wait **5 years** until the next screening test [N1-F1].  
- After both tests are **normal**, you may wait **5 years** for co-testing [N1-F1].  

But this is only true if your results are normal. If your result is **abnormal**, you should **not wait for the next scheduled test**—you should see your provider sooner, and sometimes you may need more frequent follow-up [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-F1].

## 4) When to stop cervical cancer screening and what changes the schedule
The main age threshold for stopping screening is **65 years**, but it depends on your prior screening history.  
- USPSTF says screening should **not be done** in women older than 65 years who have had **adequate prior screening** and are not otherwise at high risk [N2-F2].  
- NCBI says clinicians should stop screening average-risk women older than 65 years if they have had **3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cytology plus HPV test results within 10 years**, with the most recent test performed within 5 years [N3-F3].  
- CDC similarly says women older than 65 may not need screening if they have had **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results and no cervical precancer [N1-F1].  

So the schedule changes when:
- You reach age 65.
- You have had enough normal tests in the past.
- You have had a **hysterectomy with removal of the cervix** and no high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer [N2-F2].
- Your results are abnormal or you have other risk factors [N2-F2][N4-F2].

## 5) Practical patient guidance: how to explain the schedule in simple terms
You can explain it like this:  
- Start screening at **age 21**.  
- If you are **21–29 years old**, get a **Pap test every 3 years**.  
- If you are **30–65 years old**, you can choose **HPV testing every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years**.  
- If you are **older than 65**, you may **not need screening anymore** if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

If your result is **normal**, you can wait the full interval before your next test. If it’s **abnormal**, you should **see your provider sooner** [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 6) What to do if a Pap/HPV result is abnormal
The evidence is clear: abnormal results do **not** mean cancer, but they do mean **follow-up is needed** [N6-R3][N1-F1].  
- If your **Pap or HPV result is abnormal**, your provider will explain the next steps and determine whether you need more testing sooner [N1-F1][N6-R3].  
- If HPV is **positive**, follow-up is usually more urgent: you may need to come back **sooner** and may be referred to **colposcopy** [N4-R4].  
- ACOG also says **repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year** is recommended for minor abnormalities indicating HPV [N4-R1].  

So the next step after an abnormal result is to:
1. See your provider.
2. Follow their instructions for repeat testing or further evaluation.
3. Understand that abnormal results usually mean follow-up, not a cancer diagnosis [N6-R3][N4-R4].

## 7) When to see a provider for further evaluation
You should see a provider after an **abnormal result** or if HPV is **positive** [N4-R4][N1-F1].  
- If your result is abnormal, the provider will contact you and decide what to do next [N1-F1].  
- If HPV is positive, the provider may recommend **colposcopy** or earlier repeat testing [N4-R4].  
- If you have other risk factors, a history of abnormal results, or a hysterectomy with cervix removal, your provider may also change your schedule [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence shows that HPV status can change how you are followed.  
- **HPV-negative results** can support longer intervals and less urgent follow-up [N1-F1][N3-F3].  
- **HPV-positive results** usually mean shorter follow-up intervals, earlier repeat testing, and a higher chance of referral to **colposcopy** [N4-R4][N4-R1].  

So:
- If HPV is negative and your Pap is normal, you can wait longer before the next test.
- If HPV is positive, you may need to come back sooner and may need more testing or evaluation [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 9) Bottom line for the patient
If you want to know how often you should get the **Pap test and HPV test**, the answer is:

- **Start at age 21**.
- **21–29 years**: every **3 years** with Pap only.
- **30–65 years**: every **5 years** with HPV alone or co-testing.
- **Over 65 years**: screening may stop if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].
- **If a result is normal**, you can wait the full interval before your next test.
- **If a result is abnormal or HPV is positive**, you should see your provider sooner [N1-F1][N4-R4].

In simple terms:  
**Normal results = wait the full time. Abnormal results = see your provider sooner.**

# Final answer: How often should you get the Pap test and HPV test?

If you’re asking “no sé cada cuánto me debo hacer la prueba de Papanicolau y de HPV,” the short answer is: the schedule depends on your age and your test results, but the general guidelines are simple and clear.

## 1) Age groups and how often screening is recommended
The evidence is consistent across the guidelines.  
- **Women aged 21 to 29 years**: you should be screened every **3 years** with **Pap testing alone** [N2-F2][N1-F1].  
- **Women aged 30 to 65 years**: you can choose **HPV testing alone every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Women older than 65 years**: screening may stop if you have had **enough normal tests in the past**, usually **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

So the core schedule is:
- **21–29 years**: every 3 years with Pap only.
- **30–65 years**: every 5 years with HPV alone or co-testing.
- **Over 65 years**: screening may stop if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 2) How Pap test and HPV test intervals differ by age and co-testing status
The main difference is that **Pap-only screening is shorter than HPV-only screening** in some age groups.

- **Women aged 21–29 years**: the guidelines recommend **Pap only every 3 years**, and routine HPV testing is not recommended in this group [N1-F1][N3-F3].  
- **Women aged 30–65 years**: the choice is **HPV-only every 5 years** or **co-testing every 5 years** [N1-F1][N2-F2].  
- **Co-testing** is preferred for women aged 30–65 because it combines Pap and HPV results and may offer better reassurance in some settings [N2-F2][N3-F3].  

In other words, the interval is usually **every 3 years** if you have Pap only in younger women, and **every 5 years** if you use HPV alone or co-testing in older women [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## 3) When to repeat testing and when to skip a test
The evidence says that if your test result is **normal**, you may **wait the full interval** before the next test.  
- After a **normal Pap test alone**, you may wait **3 years** until the next Pap test [N1-F1].  
- After a **normal HPV test alone**, you may wait **5 years** until the next screening test [N1-F1].  
- After both tests are **normal**, you may wait **5 years** for co-testing [N1-F1].  

But this is only true if your results are normal. If your result is **abnormal**, you should **not wait for the next scheduled test**—you should see your provider sooner, and sometimes you may need more frequent follow-up [N4-R1][N4-R4][N1-F1].

## 4) When to stop cervical cancer screening and what changes the schedule
The main age threshold for stopping screening is **65 years**, but it depends on your prior screening history.  
- USPSTF says screening should **not be done** in women older than 65 years who have had **adequate prior screening** and are not otherwise at high risk [N2-F2].  
- NCBI says clinicians should stop screening average-risk women older than 65 years if they have had **3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative cytology plus HPV test results within 10 years**, with the most recent test performed within 5 years [N3-F3].  
- CDC similarly says women older than 65 may not need screening if they have had **at least three Pap tests or two HPV tests in the past 10 years** with normal or negative results and no cervical precancer [N1-F1].  

So the schedule changes when:
- You reach age 65.
- You have had enough normal tests in the past.
- You have had a **hysterectomy with removal of the cervix** and no high-grade precancerous lesion or cervical cancer [N2-F2].
- Your results are abnormal or you have other risk factors [N2-F2][N4-F2].

## 5) Practical patient guidance: how to explain the schedule in simple terms
You can explain it like this:  
- Start screening at **age 21**.  
- If you are **21–29 years old**, get a **Pap test every 3 years**.  
- If you are **30–65 years old**, you can choose **HPV testing every 5 years** or **Pap and HPV co-testing every 5 years**.  
- If you are **older than 65**, you may **not need screening anymore** if you’ve had enough normal tests [N1-F1][N2-F2].  

If your result is **normal**, you can wait the full interval before your next test. If it’s **abnormal**, you should **see your provider sooner** [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## 6) What to do if a Pap/HPV result is abnormal
The evidence is clear: abnormal results do **not** mean cancer, but they do mean **follow-up is needed** [N6-R3][N1-F1].  
- If your **Pap or HPV result is abnormal**, your provider will explain the next steps and determine whether you need more testing sooner [N1-F1][N6-R3].  
- If HPV is **positive**, follow-up is usually more urgent: you may need to come back **sooner** and may be referred to **colposcopy** [N4-R4].  
- ACOG also says **repeat HPV testing or co-testing at 1 year** is recommended for minor abnormalities indicating HPV [N4-R1].  

So the next step after an abnormal result is to:
1. See your provider.
2. Follow their instructions for repeat testing or further evaluation.
3. Understand that abnormal results usually mean follow-up, not a cancer diagnosis [N6-R3][N4-R4].

## 7) When to see a provider for further evaluation
You should see a provider after an **abnormal result** or if HPV is **positive** [N4-R4][N1-F1].  
- If your result is abnormal, the provider will contact you and decide what to do next [N1-F1].  
- If HPV is positive, the provider may recommend **colposcopy** or earlier repeat testing [N4-R4].

The main difference is that **Pap-only screening is shorter than HPV-only screening** in some age groups.

The evidence says that if your test result is **normal**, you may **wait the full interval** before the next test.
